Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 2 (mod 7), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 1. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 3), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ∈ {0, 2}. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 3), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ∈ {0, 2}. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 3) and |A| = 4, and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ∈ {0, 2}. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 3), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 1 (mod 3) and |A ∩ B| ∈ {0, 2}. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 7), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ∈ {0, 2}. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 2·y = z, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 2·y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that A contains no x, y, z with x ≠ y and x + y = 2z, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 3·y = 2·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.

Let Z_n be the integers modulo n. Consider subsets A ⊆ Z_n such that A contains no x, y, z with x ≠ y and x + y = 2z, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 3·y = 2·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 3), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 1 (mod 3). Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Extremal families look like a common core plus disjoint blocks. At n=8 the core is {8}, the blocks are {2,3,6} and {4,5,7}, and the family is the core joined with every union of blocks (4 sets). Each block has size 3, which is 0 mod 3, so every set has size 1 mod 3 and every pairwise intersection is core plus blocks, also 1 mod 3. Using k blocks needs 1+3k elements and gives 2^k sets. This fits the data:

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 3), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 1 (mod 3). Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Sets of size 0 or 1 mod 3 that pairwise meet in 1 mod 3 are mostly triples meeting in exactly one point, i.e. linear 3-uniform families. At n=7 the Fano plane's 7 lines are extremal. At n=8 one line L is replaced by L plus the new point, a 4-set. Every other line meets L in exactly one point, so the family still has 7 members. Smaller n have only partial linear triple systems, e.g. 4 sets at n=6.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 1 (mod 3). Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Observed f(n)=n for n=3..8. The n=8 extremal family is two blocks. Block one: {1,x} for x=3,5,7,8, pairwise meeting exactly in {1}. Block two: core C={3,5,7,8} (|C|=4≡1 mod 3) and C plus one private element (2, 4 or 6), pairwise meeting in C. Each {1,x} meets each block-two set in {x}, size 1. So every intersection has size 1 or 4, both ≡1 mod 3. The values fit a linear bound f(n)=n, but this is only checked for n≤8.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 3) and |A| = 4, and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 1 (mod 3). Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Members are 4-sets, and any two must meet in exactly 1 element, since intersections of size 4 are impossible for distinct sets and sizes 0, 2 and 3 are excluded. So F is a family of 4-sets pairwise meeting in exactly one point. Two such sets need 7 points, which gives f(7)=2 and f(8)=2. For n≤6 two sets cannot fit, so f=1 for n=4,5,6 and f=0 for n=3. In the n=8 example, {2,3,6,8} and {4,5,7,8} share only point 8.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 2), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 1 (mod 2). Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.

Let Z_n be the integers modulo n. Consider subsets A ⊆ Z_n such that the sums a + b over unordered pairs {a, b} ⊆ A (a = b allowed) are pairwise distinct, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with 3·x + 3·y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: A is a Sidon set in Z_n (all sums a+b distinct, doubles included) that also avoids 3x+3y=3z for non-all-equal x,y,z. f grows slowly, roughly like sqrt(n) at most. It is non-monotone: it dips at n=12 and n=21, both multiples of 3, where the condition 3x+3y=3z only constrains classes mod n/3 and is easier to violate. The extremal n=30 set {1,3,7,15} has doubling-type gaps. Thresholds: 1 at n=4, 2 for n=5..10, 3 from n=11, 4 from n=19. These patterns are observed,

statement: Let Z_n be the integers modulo n. Consider subsets A ⊆ Z_n such that A contains no x, y, z (not necessarily distinct) with x + y = z, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with 3·x + 3·y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: For even n, f(n)=n/2. The extremal set is the odd residues, which is sum-free because odd+odd is even. The 3x+3y=3z condition also fails, since x+y−z is odd and so not a multiple of n/3. For odd n, f(n) matches the classical maximum sum-free size in Z_n, given by cosets of middle-third intervals. If n has a prime factor p≡2 (mod 3), f(n)=(p+1)/3·n/p for the smallest such p. If 3|n but no such p exists, f(n)=n/3. Otherwise f(n)=(n−1)/3. This is fitted

statement: Let Z_n be the integers modulo n. Consider subsets A ⊆ Z_n such that the sums a + b over unordered pairs {a, b} ⊆ A (a = b allowed) are pairwise distinct, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 2·y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: A is a Sidon set in Z_n (all sums a+b distinct, a=b allowed) that also has no nontrivial solution of x+2y=3z. Any 2-element set works, so f=2 for small n. Size 3 first fits at n=13, size 4 at n=20 and from n=24 on. The size-4 Sidon condition needs about 4·5/2=10 distinct sums, so n must be large enough. The dips at n=21, 22, 23 are probably from arithmetic obstructions at those moduli. {0,1,4,9} is a Sidon set with increasing

statement: Let Z_n be the integers modulo n. Consider subsets A ⊆ Z_n such that A contains no x, y, z with x ≠ y and x + y = 2z, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with 3·x + 3·y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: Since 3x+3y=3z means x+y≡z mod n/gcd(n,3), A must be sum-free (no Schur triples) as well as 3-AP-free. When 3∤n this is mod n. When 3|n the sum-free condition is on residues mod n/3, so extremal sets are lifts of small sum-free, AP-free residue sets. At n=30, A is residues {1,4,6,9} mod 15, each taken twice (1,16; 4,19; 6,21; 9,24). Values are small and irregular, larger for n=10, 22, 26, 28, 30.

statement: Let Z_n be the integers modulo n. Consider subsets A ⊆ Z_n such that A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 2·y = 2·z, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with 3·x + 3·y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that A contains no x, y, z (not necessarily distinct) with x + y = z, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 2·y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: The n=30 extremal set is {a ≤ 27 : a mod 11 ∈ {1,3,5}}, three blocks {1,3,5}+11k for k=0,1,2. Pairwise sums of the residues {1,3,5} are 2,4,6,8,10 mod 11, so they never land back in {1,3,5}. That makes the set sum-free, and the x+2y=3z condition also seems to fail. This looks like a periodic residue-class construction, with f rising in steps and then staying at 9 for n=21..30. I have not proved optimality; this is read off the brute-force data.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that A contains no x, y, z (not necessarily distinct) with x + y = z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: f(n) = ⌈n/2⌉ for these n (4 to 30). Lower bound: the odd numbers in [n] are sum-free, since the sum of two odds is even. Upper bound: let m be the largest element of A. For each pair {a, m−a} with a < m, at most one lies in A, and m/2 is excluded when m is even, because m/2 + m/2 = m. Counting then gives |A| ≤ ⌈n/2⌉. Other extremal sets exist, such as the upper half

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + y = 2·z, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 2·y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: A must avoid nontrivial 3-term APs (x+y=2z) and nontrivial solutions of x+2y=3z, so it is a Salem–Spencer-type set with an extra weighted-mean restriction. f is a nondecreasing step function that grows slowly. It stays flat for long stretches (4 for n=7–11, 8 for n=22–28) and rises by 1 when a new valid set fits. Extremal sets are irregular, with clustered pairs, e.g. {1,2,5,6,15,17,26,27,30}. I have not derived a closed form.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with 2·x + y = z, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 2·y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: The n=30 extremal set is {x ≤ 30 : x mod 11 ∈ {1,2,7}}, a periodic residue-class set of density 3/11. Mod 11, the residue set {1,2,7} appears to avoid both 2x+y=z and x+2y=3z, so no solutions arise without wraparound either. This suggests f(n) grows roughly like 3n/11 (9 at n=30). For smaller n, e.g. n=21 with f=8, extremal sets are irregular and exceed this pattern. The values are plateaus with unit jumps, which I did not prove.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that A contains no x, y, z (not necessarily distinct) with x + y = z, and all sums a + b with a, b ∈ A and a ≤ b are distinct. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 5), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 4 (mod 5). Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: For n ≤ 7, f=1: a second set would need size 6 (or 1) and meet the first in 4 mod 5 elements, which cannot fit in so few points. At n=8, partition [8] into four pairs {12},{34},{56},{78}. The extremal family is the four 6-sets, each the complement of one pair. Each has size 6 ≡ 1 mod 5. Any two meet in 8−4 = 4 elements, so ≡ 4 mod 5. Hence f(8)=4.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 5), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 4 (mod 5) and |A ∩ B| = 0. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Distinct members would need |A∩B| ≡ 4 (mod 5) and |A∩B| = 0, which contradict each other (0 is not ≡ 4). So no two distinct members can coexist, and F has at most one set. A single set with |A| ≡ 1 (mod 5), such as a 6-set (or a singleton), satisfies the conditions vacuously. Hence f(n) = 1 whenever such a set exists. The n=8 example is one 6-set.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 4 (mod 5). Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Extremal family at n=8: all six 5-subsets of the 6-set {2,3,4,6,7,8}. Any two distinct ones meet in exactly 4 elements, which is ≡ 4 mod 5. So n=6 already gives 6 sets (the 5-subsets of [6]), and f stays 6 for n=7 and n=8 because no larger family fits. For n≤4 only a single set fits, and n=5 allows two. This is a structural description of the data, not a proof of the upper bounds.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 5), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 1 or 4 (mod 5). Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Correction to my earlier reply: the n=8 example is valid. Members have size 1 or 6. Distinct singletons meet in 0, which is not allowed, so at most one singleton fits. For n≤5 no 6-set exists, so f=1. At n=6, a singleton inside the full set gives 2, and n=7 gives no more. At n=8, {8} together with {7,8}∪(two of the three disjoint pairs {1,2},{3,4},{5,6}) gives 4. The singleton meets each 6-set in 1, and two 6-sets meet in 4.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 5), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| ≡ 4 (mod 5). Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that all sums a + b with a, b ∈ A and a ≤ b are distinct. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: A is a Sidon set (B2 set): all sums a+b with a≤b are distinct, equivalently all positive differences are distinct, so A is a Golomb ruler with marks in [n]. f(n) is the largest number of marks k such that an optimal k-mark Golomb ruler has length ≤ n−1. Jumps occur at n=4,7,12,18,26, matching optimal ruler lengths 3,6,11,17,25 for k=3,...,7. The n=30 example {1,2,4,9,13,23,29} is a 7-mark ruler with differences all distinct.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with 2·x + y = 2·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: f(n) = ceil(n/2) = floor((n+1)/2) for n ≥ 4. The extremal example is the set of odd numbers. In 2x+y=2z, y = 2(z−x) must be even, so an all-odd set has no solution, which gives |A| ≥ ceil(n/2). The matching upper bound is only checked by brute force up to n = 30, not proved here. Other extremal sets may exist.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: The data fit f(n) = ⌈n/2⌉ for n ≥ 5. The exception in the data is f(4) = 3, which is above ⌈4/2⌉ = 2. The extremal example is the set of all odd numbers in [n]. For odd x, y, z, the sum x+y is even and 3z is odd, so x+y = 3z cannot hold. This gives ⌈n/2⌉ elements. I have not proved the matching upper bound. It is supported only by the brute-force values.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 2·y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: A must avoid nontrivial solutions of x+2y=3z, meaning z is the weighted mean (x+2y)/3 of distinct x,y (x≡y mod 3 needed). Extremal sets look like small-element clusters plus large-element clusters with gaps, e.g. {1,2,3,6,9} and {17,18,22,27,28,29}. f is a nondecreasing step function with plateaus, growing slowly (roughly sublinear). This is a pattern fitted to the data, not a proof.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}, with ordinary integer addition (no wraparound). Consider subsets A ⊆ [n] such that all sums a + b with a, b ∈ A and a ≤ b are distinct, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + y = 3·z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 3), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 1. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Extremal families are sunflowers with a one-element kernel: all members share one point x (here 8) and are otherwise pairwise disjoint. Sizes are 1, 4, 7, …, so the cheapest family is {x} plus k disjoint petals of 3 new points each (sets of size 4). That needs 1+3k ≤ n, so f = 1 + ⌊(n−1)/3⌋, which gives 1,2,2,2,3,3 for n=3..8. The data fit this pattern, but this is not a proof of optimality.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 3) and |A| = 4, and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 1. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Members are 4-sets (4 ≡ 1 mod 3) pairwise meeting in exactly one point. f(n)=0 for n<4, and a single 4-set gives f=1 for n=4,5,6. Two 4-sets sharing exactly one point need 4+4-1=7 points, so f(7)=f(8)=2, e.g. {2,3,6,8},{4,5,7,8}: two blocks glued at one common element. A third set meeting both in exactly one point needs more points than 8 allows here, so f stays 2 through n=8.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 2), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 1. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: At n=7 the extremal family is the Fano plane: 7 triples (lines), any two meeting in exactly one point. The n=8 example is a Fano plane on {2,...,8} with point 1 unused, so f(8)=f(7)=7. For n=5 and n=6 the extremal families are smaller, such as sunflower or near-pencil types with a common point and disjoint even-size petals. I have not proved the upper bounds. f is nondecreasing, since an unused point can be added, and it jumps when a Fano-like

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 1. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: f(n)=n for 3≤n≤8, matching the nonuniform Fisher-type bound (Majumdar/Deza–Frankl–Singhi): families with all pairwise intersections of size exactly 1 have at most n members. Extremal example: the star of pairs {1,i}, i=2..n, plus the complementary set {2,…,n}. It meets each pair {1,i} only in i. That gives (n−1)+1=n sets. Other extremal families exist, e.g. projective-plane-type ones.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 (mod 7), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 1. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.

Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 2 (mod 3), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 3. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Members have size 5 for n ≤ 8, because size 2 is too small and size 8 would leave no room for another member meeting it in 3 points. Take complements in [n]. Two 5-sets meet in exactly 3 points iff their complements have union of size n−3. For n ≤ 6 no two 5-sets work, so f = 1. For n = 7 the complements are pairwise disjoint 2-sets, so f(7) = 3. statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 3. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Pairwise intersections all equal 3, so Fisher-type (Deza/Frankl–Füredi) bounds give f(n) ≤ n. Small cases: f(3)=1 and f(4)=2 (a 3-set plus a 4-set containing it). f(5)=5 is all five 4-subsets of [5], which pairwise meet in 3. At n=6 and n=7 nothing beats this, so f stays 5. At n=8 the extremal family has 7 sets: all contain 8, and removing 8 leaves one 3-set and six 4-sets of [7] pairwise meeting in 2, a design-like structure. This gives n−1=7.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 2 (mod 5), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 3. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: Allowed sizes are 2, 7, 12, ... A set of size 2 cannot meet another set in 3 points, so any family with two or more members uses sizes at least 7. Two distinct 7-sets meeting in exactly 3 points need at least 7+7-3 = 11 points. For n ≤ 8 this is impossible, so at most one set fits. A single set has no pairs to check, so it is valid. statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 0 or 2 (mod 3), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 3. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.
explanation: At n=8 the extremal family has a common point 8, plus the 7 complements of Fano-plane lines in [7]. These are 4-sets pairwise meeting in exactly 2 points, a symmetric 2-(7,4,2) design. Adding 8 gives 5-sets (5≡2 mod 3) pairwise meeting in exactly 3. The size 7 matches an n-1 style bound for exact-intersection families (Fisher/Ray-Chaudhuri–Wilson type). For n≤7 no such design fits, so f stays small (1,1,2,2,3). I did not prove the small cases.

statement: Let [n] = {1,…,n}. Consider families F of distinct subsets of [n] such that every member A has |A| ≡ 1 or 2 (mod 3), and any two distinct members A ≠ B have |A ∩ B| = 3. Let f(n) be the largest possible |F|.

Let Z_n be the integers modulo n. Consider subsets A ⊆ Z_n such that A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + y = 2·z, and A contains no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + 3·y = z. Let f(n) be the largest possible |A|.
explanation: A has no nontrivial 3-term progression (x+y=2z) and no nontrivial solution of z=x+3y. f(n) grows slowly, roughly n/6, and is non-monotone: it dips at n=19 and 22 and rises at n=18, 21, 24 and 30. Highly composite n do best. Extremal sets are small and spread out. At n=30, {1,2,9,11,18,19} avoids both patterns. The values come from brute-force search, and I have no closed form.
